claim: Contamination is implicated in almost all retail slip accidents; cleaning itself can create slippery floors
transfer: Mechanism plausible for children; no effect size
implication: Prioritize source control, cleaning method and response time

claim: Signs and cones only warn of a hazard; they do not prevent entry
transfer: Directly relevant: children do not read signs
implication: Isolation means a physical barrier or closure plus an accessible alternative

claim: ADA accessible surfaces must be stable, firm and slip resistant; no minimum friction value is set
setting: U.S. sites covered by the ADA
transfer: Applies to all visitors including children with disabilities
basis: Regulation text (unofficial copy) and agency guide
limits: Coverage and stricter local rules decided locally
implication: Do not cite an "ADA friction number"; specialists set method-specific thresholds

claim: ADA carpet rules: securely attached, firm or no cushion, pile ≤ 1/2 in, exposed edges trimmed
limits: Whether a product is "carpet" and whether the area is covered must be decided
implication: Soft or cushioned coverings on routes need access review before purchase

claim: ADA changes in level: ≤ 1/4 in vertical; ≤ 1/2 in bevelled at 1:2 maximum; larger changes ramped
transfer: Applies to mat, underlay and padding edges
implication: Measure every new edge and transition at commissioning

claim: ADA protruding objects: 27–80 in leading edges protrude ≤ 4 in; protrusions may not reduce required clear width; 80 in headroom
implication: Check guard thickness at the real fixture

claim: ADA accessible route clear width 36 in, reducible to 32 in for ≤ 24 in
transfer: Padding on aisle fixtures can narrow routes
limits: Other width rules (turns, passing spaces) also apply
implication: Measure route width after guards are fitted

claim: Accessible features must be maintained; isolated or temporary interruptions for maintenance or repair are allowed; DOJ expects merchandise retrieval when an aisle is blocked
transfer: Shapes how closures and isolations are run
implication: Isolation procedure includes assistance and prompt reopening

claim: U.S. employers must inspect walking-working surfaces and correct or guard hazards before employees use them; no friction number
implication: Use as the worker-safety floor; customer duties need counsel

claim: Ontario guidance: give public notice of temporary disruptions to accessible facilities, with reason, duration and alternatives
transfer: Applies to closures during installation or isolation
implication: Add notices to the installation and closure procedures for Ontario sites

claim: Tribometer validation (F2508-23) is not intended to establish a safe threshold
implication: Thresholds must be set by specialists before testing

claim: Playground surfacing test F1292-26 is specific to head-injury risk in playground use zones; laboratory results ignore aging and maintenance
implication: Never cite playground certification for retail floors or fixtures

claim: Floor-covering fire method E648-25a was developed for corridors and exitways and is not alone a fire-hazard assessment
limits: Required class comes from the adopted code
implication: Fixture padding needs its own code determination

claim: A randomized trial of compliant flooring found no effect on serious fall injuries; falls were non-significantly higher; harms were not assessed
setting: Older adults, one long-term care site
implication: Do not claim cushioning efficacy for children or retail

claim: Compliant flooring reduces laboratory impact forces but may raise fall risk and increases force to move wheeled equipment
implication: Rolling effort and stability are pass/fail criteria

claim: An average of about 24,000 U.S. children under 15 a year were treated in emergency departments for shopping-cart injuries (1990–2011); most involved the head
implication: Route cart controls to an owner (task T35) before buying floor products

claim: For children under five, falls from carts were 82% of cart injuries and tip-overs 4%; 84% involved the head or face
implication: Prioritize restraint use and cart condition

claim: Cart-related concussion/closed-head-injury rates rose 1990–2011 and totals did not fall after the 2004 cart standard
implication: A design standard alone is not enough; operational controls matter

claim: The shopping-cart standard F2372-15(2021) covers carts and restraints for children 6 months–4 years and excludes infant carriers
implication: Use as a procurement criterion when replacing carts

claim: A store-entrance intervention raised correct cart-restraint use from 15% to 49%; about half remained unrestrained
limits: Injuries not measured; primary article not retrieved
implication: Candidate operational control to evaluate, not an injury claim

claim: A multi-component hospital-employee program was followed by 58% fewer slip, trip and fall claims
transfer: Partial: housekeeping parts may transfer; footwear does not
implication: Supports operational controls; not a customer estimate

claim: No controlled study of retail edge guards or corner padding was found in this targeted review
implication: Treat guards as an untested residual-hazard option

claim: WHO 97th-percentile height is about 92–93 cm at age two and 118–119 cm at age five
implication: Basis for the survey band below

claim: Survey fixture edges from the floor to at least 120 cm for ages two to five
limits: Raise for older children; not a legal requirement
implication: Use in the hazard walk (document 28)

claim: Use a 90-day operational feasibility window after commissioning
implication: Agree locally; extend if needed

claim: At 2 events per 100,000 entries, detecting a 20% reduction needs about 355 comparison events (about 17.7 million entries per arm)
basis: Normal approximation for a log rate ratio
implication: A single-site pilot cannot support an injury-reduction claim

claim: 15,000 initial cost and 20,000 retained loss scenario
implication: Replace with quotes and validated loss data

claim: Local injury reduction and insurance savings
implication: No public benefit claim; premium changes excluded from models

claim: U.S. disabled-access tax mechanisms exist with eligibility limits (credit for small businesses; deduction up to $15,000 a year)
limits: Eligibility of this work not established
implication: Tax review before any budget recognition

claim: Research is defined by systematic investigation for generalizable knowledge (U.S.); TCPS 2 treats pilot studies as research requiring REB review
implication: Obtain a determination before structured testing or evaluation

claim: Video surveillance: consider less intrusive alternatives, limit to purpose, notify, secure and delete
implication: No new CCTV for this program; footage stays in protected systems

claim: Code editions depend on adoption and timing (2025 California code for permits from 1 Jan 2026; Ontario 2024 code for new construction and extensive renovation; 2025 national model codes published)
limits: Local amendments and project scope decide
implication: Record edition and basis per requirement in the jurisdiction register

claim: The FDA Food Code 2026 edition was released on 17 September 2026 as a model code
limits: Adoption varies; floor provisions not audited
implication: Health authority confirms the adopted text for food zones

claim: Falls are the second leading cause of unintentional injury death worldwide, and nearly 40% of the disability-adjusted life years lost to falls occur in children
transfer: Shows the scale of child falls; says nothing about retail's share
implication: Child falls are a legitimate public-health priority; measure the retail share locally before claiming it

claim: Falls are a leading cause of non-fatal child injury but account for a small share of child injury deaths
transfer: Supports measuring non-fatal outcomes; retail share unknown
basis: WHO/UNICEF report chapter and news release
implication: Plan evaluations around non-fatal injuries and hazards, not deaths

claim: In 2008 there was insufficient trial evidence that environmental changes in homes reduce the number of child injuries
transfer: Caution transfers: environmental change is plausible but unproven
implication: Present site changes as reasonable precautions under evaluation, never as proven injury reductions

claim: CRPD States Parties must take measures so that facilities open to the public, including privately run ones, take accessibility into account, and must consult disabled people, including disabled children
limits: Obligations fall on States, not businesses; ratification and national law vary
implication: No child-safety change may reduce access; consult disability organizations before changing a site

claim: A safe and healthy working environment has been an ILO fundamental principle since 2022
transfer: Retail cleaning, cart handling and ergonomics
implication: Worker safety is part of every assessment, not a side issue

claim: ISO 21542 (building accessibility) and ISO/IEC Guide 50 (child safety in product standards) are useful reference points; their public scopes do not describe retail child-impact thresholds
implication: Cite them as references in local reviews; never as an approval or a threshold
